title: Chapter 30 – We Only Hold It
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

Father carries Grandfather down.

He does it without a word, with the old man's arm over his shoulder and the other beneath his knees, as he once carried Jian down from the roof of the granary. The Patriarch of Green Pine weighs less than a child. His robe hangs from him in folds. The red-gold light has gone out of his skin, and what is left is a gray, papery, extraordinarily peaceful face, with the white hair spread across Wenyuan's sleeve.

Mother carries Jian. He has told her twice that he can walk. She has not answered either time.

The stair is cold.

That is the first thing he notices, and for a long while the only thing. The upper steps were always cold. The lower steps were warm: a faint, living, animal warmth that rose to meet the feet. Tonight the cold goes all the way down. At the twentieth step it has not eased. At the thirtieth his breath makes a cloud in the lamplight. At the thirty-fifth, he stops looking for the hum.

It's gone.

The fragment, sewn into his collar, lies against his skin as dead as a pebble. The hill is silent. There is no vein. The great slow tide that has run beneath Green Pine for a hundred and fifty years, that fed the pines and the spring and every Qi-heavy breath the Lins ever drew, has gone out like water out of a bath.

He burned it. The thought comes with perfect, unfeeling clarity. Grandfather's fire drew on the vein as well. All of it. For one hour, the whole hill was a candle.

"Here," says Grandfather.

They have reached the foot of the fortieth step.

"Put me down. By the wall. There."

Father lowers him against the stone, a hand's breadth from the plain dark step with its invisible tracery of lines. The old man settles with a long breath, like a man sitting down at the end of a day's work. The lamp in Mother's hand throws a small yellow room round the four of them, and beyond it the round chamber is black and cold. The basin is dry. The cushion has not moved.

Lin Jian lets Mother set him down at Grandfather's side. She goes on her knees on the other.

```
[Scan — Lin Zhenshan]
Ember fire: dying (12% of peak)
Life force: 2% (and falling)
Injuries: ribs 5 broken, left lung punctured, liver ruptured (internal), meridian burn 80%
Estimated time to cessation: under 30 minutes
```

He reads it once. He does not read it again.

* * *

"Wenyuan," says Grandfather.

Father kneels. His hands, which carried the old man down forty steps without a tremor, are shaking now, and he clasps them on his knees to keep them still. "Father."

"It's yours."

"Father."

"The hill, the house, the sword. All of it. I wrote your name in the Hall's book in the spring, and I read it out to Mo like a fool. The Compact will take until autumn to confirm it. Until then you are only the man who happens to be standing in my chair." The dry humor flickers, and fades. "Stand in it anyway."

"It's enough," says Father, hoarsely. "You've done enough."

"It isn't. It never is." The old man lifts a hand, with great effort, and lays it on his son's wrist. "Listen to me. Heng will come back. Not soon; his dantian is broken, and a Foundation Establishment cultivator with a broken dantian is a long time mending. Three years. Five. Perhaps more. But he will come, and he will come with something better than hired men and a shield block." A breath, a thin one. "Use the years."

"How?"

"Send Feng to the Sect. The Outer Court takes triple-root disciples up to the age of thirty, and the young man has the talent for it. He will learn there what none of us can teach him, and he will be a Lin inside their walls, which is worth more than any pin. Mend the shop. Mend the books, and the walls, and..." The faintest crook of the mouth. "Yourself. Third Aunt will tell you what you need. Old Hu's book may have more in it than one formula. Ask him about the rest."

Father does not answer. His head is bowed so low that his hair hides his face.

"Don't be proud," says Grandfather. "Be careful. Be patient. Hold on. That is all a patriarch is, in the end. A man who does not let go."

"I'll try."

"You will do better than I did. You have never needed to be told twice." The hand slides from his wrist. "Qinghe."

Mother's eyes are dry. It is the hardest thing Lin Jian has ever seen. "Father."

"I opposed the marriage."

"I know."

"I said some things to Wenyuan about road-wanderers." The old man looks at her. His eyes are very clear. "I was wrong in every particular. You were the best thing that ever came up that road. If I could, I would walk back down it and thank whoever sent you."

Mother makes a small sound.

"Keep holding it," says Grandfather softly. "You know how. You always have."

"I will."

"Good." He lets his head rest against the wall. "Now go up, both of you. Go and stand. There are people at the top of the stair who need a Patriarch more than I need an audience. Jian stays."

Father hesitates. "Father..."

"Wenyuan." It is the old voice, the one that used to carry across the training yard at dawn, and it brings Father to his feet before he knows it. "Go and stand."

For a moment longer he does not move. Then he bends, and does something Lin Jian has never seen in his life: he lays his forehead against his father's, and holds it there. Neither of them says anything. Then he lifts the old plain sword from the stone, where it lay at the old man's side. He looks at it. He lays it back on the floor of the chamber.

"I'll come for it," says Father. "Later."

Mother kisses Lin Jian once, hard, on the top of the head. She goes up the stairs behind her husband without looking back.

Then there is only the lamp, and the cold, and the old man.

* * *

"Your arm," says Grandfather, after a while.

"It will mend."

"Will it?"

Lin Jian looks down at the limp thing hanging in his sleeve and lets the panel tell him.

```
[Host status — Lin Jian]

"Yes," he says. "Three weeks. Perhaps five."

"Good." The old man closes his eyes, and for a long moment Lin Jian thinks he has gone. Then: "You didn't ask me."

"I know."

"I would have told you."

"I know." The words come out rough. "That's why I didn't."

A faint, dry sound, which in a healthier man might have been a laugh. The lamp flickers. Behind them the chamber is black, and the cold has found its way into Lin Jian's bones.

"I told you something once," says Grandfather. "Seventeen years ago, the night after you were born. I was sitting in the hall with your father, drinking more than I should, and he said, Father, the child looked at me. And I said: Wenyuan, children look. And he said: No. He looked at me as if he were checking that I was real." The lined face moves. "I did not understand him. I went to the cradle, in the end. You were asleep. I looked at you for an hour. And I thought: this one is going to be trouble."

"Feng says that."

"Feng is a clever boy. He got it from me." A pause. "I never told anyone what my grandfather said to me, in the end. I am going to tell you."

Lin Jian waits.

"I told you the first part. The hill is not ours. We only hold it. He said more. He said: There is a door under the hill."

The words sit in the cold air like stones.

"He found it the year he took the hill from the wolves. A door, in the rock below the chamber, where the vein comes up. He did not open it. He did not know how. But he sat beside it, every night, for seventeen years, with his back to the wall where I am sitting now, and the vein poured into him as if he were a cup, and in nine years he was Foundation Establishment. A man who had been Qi Refining Six when he came to the hill." The old voice is very quiet. "It is older than the Sect. He said it was older than anything. He spent forty years hiding it, from his sons, from the Hall, from the world. And he told me: The step will answer one day. Not to me, nor to you. When it does, that one will decide."

The lamp hisses.

"I have put my hand in the print every year for a hundred years," says Lin Zhenshan. "The autumn festival. Every year, I knelt and I asked, and every year the stone was cold. I thought: I am the wrong one. I thought: It will be my son. I thought: Perhaps it will be Feng, in his turn. Then you were born, and looked at your father as if you were checking he was real."

His eyes open.

"Put your hand in the print, Jian."

Lin Jian does not breathe.

"The left. The other is no use."

He moves, on his knees, across the stone floor to the foot of the fortieth step. The dark basalt waits. In the lamplight it is only a stone. He lays the palm of his left hand over the print of Lin Shoucheng's hand, and it is a fit, an exact fit, as a key slides into a lock.

Nothing happens.

He waits. A breath. Another. The stone is cold. The fragment is cold.

Of course not. It's been dead for three—

Warmth.

Not hot. Not even warm, at first. A faint, faint softening of the cold beneath his palm, as if a tiny ember had been laid under the stone, a thing that has no right to be there. Then it spreads. It runs out from under his hand along the surface, thin as thread. And under his collar, against his skin, the fragment wakes.

It is the first living thing the hill has done since noon. It hums, once, a single clear note, and the lines on the step begin to glow.

They are silver. They are not the pale, shy tracery that the lamp raked out of the stone. They are bright, a spiderweb of silver light from edge to edge, and they pour toward his hand and away from it, in whorls and loops and long curving strokes, filling the step with a slow, shifting pattern that is half a spiral, half a net. They run to the very border of the stone and stop, a hand's width short of the edge, as if the stone were the lid of a box and they were the writing on the lid.

```

A lock. The word goes through him like cold water. Not a door. A lock. And I have the key.

He takes his hand away. The light fades from the lines, slowly, like a coal going out, and the step is only a stone again.

Beside him, Grandfather has not made a sound. When Lin Jian looks up, the old man is watching him with an expression he has never seen before. It is not surprise. It is something closer to relief.

"Ah," says Lin Zhenshan. "So it's you."

Lin Jian doesn't answer. He can't.

"Then listen." The old man's voice has dropped to a thread. "Two things. First. Do not open it. Not yet. You are seventeen years old, and whatever is under there has been waiting for a very long time. It can wait a little longer. Open it when you are strong enough to hold what comes out. I do not know what that is. Neither did he. But he knew it was not for the weak."

"I understand."

"Second. Heng's grandfather came here once. He guessed. He told his grandson. Heng has had a hundred and seventy years to think about it. He has failed tonight, but he does not fail twice for the same reason. He will remember your face."

"I know."

"Then be ready." The old hand finds his, on the floor between them. It is cold now, and light, and still. "Be what you are, little builder. Hide it. And build."

"Grandfather..."

"I chose your name, you know. Wenyuan wanted another. He said the boy should be called something strong, like a mountain. I said: no, he is going to be a sword. A jian. A thing made on an anvil, by someone who knew what it was for." The ghost of a smile. "I do not say I was right. Only that I chose it."

Lin Jian's eyes have gone hot and blurred. He can't see the old man's face.

"I'll hold it," he says. His voice breaks on the words. "I'll hold the hill. I promise."

"That's good, little builder," says Lin Zhenshan. "That's good."

He closes his eyes.

Lin Jian counts.

He doesn't mean to. It is what he does with numbers that matter: one breath, in the silence, a long thin pull of air; two; three. The lamp gutters. The cold presses in. Four, five, six, each farther from the last. Seven. He is holding the old man's hand with his good one, and it is not a hand anymore, only a kind of weather, a fading warmth that lies in his palm like the memory of sun.

Ten. Eleven. Twelve.

Thirteen.

There is no fourteen.

* * *

He sits there a long time.

Longer than he knows. The lamp burns down to a small blue bead, and the dark comes in, and the cold, and still he sits with the old hand in his, saying nothing, thinking nothing, a small boy on the floor of a stone chamber beside the body of a very old man.

Then, some time later, he finds that he is crying.

He does not make a sound. The tears simply come, out of the blackness, one after the other, down his cheeks and over his chin and onto the cold stone. It is the first time he has wept since he came to this world. In his other life, he did not have a grandfather's hand to hold, and when the last of his people died, there had been a form to sign. He had signed it. He had gone back to work.

He had not known it could be like this. That grief is not an absence, but a weight, a stone laid on the chest by someone who loved you, and that the only way to carry it is to carry it.

I'll hold it, he thinks. I'll hold it.

After a while he lays the old hand carefully on the old chest. He looks at the white head, the closed eyes, the peaceful face of a man who has finished.

Then he gets up, and takes the lamp, and climbs.

* * *

They are waiting at the hut.

Not just Father. All of them. The yard is full of Lins, standing in the thin gold light of late afternoon: the cousins, the village guards, the women from the cellar, even Third Aunt with her medicine chest, and the old cook, Nan, with a ladle in her hand. They stand in a ragged ring around the stone hut, in the place where the great blue ring of pins burned an hour ago, now only a handful of cracked black stumps in the dust.

The children have been let out of the granary. Lin Yue stands at the back of the crowd, in a clean tunic, with her fern crown on her head, holding Aunt Meirong's hand, and her face is very serious.

Nobody says anything.

Father stands at the front, at the door. He is looking at Lin Jian. He has been looking at the door since the moment it opened.

Lin Jian comes out into the light. The sun hurts his eyes. He is carrying the lamp, absurdly, and his right arm is in a sling that someone has fastened without his noticing, and there are tear tracks, dried and stiff, down both his cheeks.

"Jian'er," says Father.

"He's gone."

Lin Wenyuan closes his eyes.

It is the only sign. He stands there with his shoulders very straight in the thin light, for the space of three heartbeats, and the yard holds its breath around him. Then he opens them again.

He turns and looks at the faces. He has known them all his life. He has bled with them and quarreled with them, and sat up through the nights of their fevers. He sees the ring of them, tired and burned and dusty, standing in a ruined yard with the crack of dried blood on their hands.

"Lin Zhenshan," he says, "Patriarch of the Lin Clan of Green Pine Hill, is dead."

Someone among the cousins begins, very quietly, to cry.

"He died as he lived. He held the hill." Father's voice does not rise. It is as dry as paper, and perfectly steady. "He asked me to tell you one thing. He said: Go and stand."

A long silence.

"Ring the bell," says Wenyuan. "Nine times, slowly. Send Wenshi to Willow Ford for a healer and the arbiter; I want them here by morning. Have the Zhao dead brought in from the road. Bury them decently, by themselves, with a marker. They are somebody's sons. Third Aunt, the wounded to the hall, those who can walk to the kitchen for something hot." A breath. "And the woman. The one Qinghe took alive. Hold her in the east wing. Do not hurt her. I want her questioned, by me, tomorrow."

He looks at them, one by one.

"That is all. I know there is much more. We will do it. But not tonight."

For a moment nothing happens.

Then Uncle Mao, big and grimy and swaying, with a torn sleeve and a long cut down one cheek, steps forward out of the crowd and goes down on one knee.

"Patriarch," he says.

It is a hoarse, rough, unmistakable word. It goes through the yard like a stone through water. And one by one, they follow. The cousins, the guards, the old women, Third Aunt, Old Nan with her ladle. They go to their knees in the dust, all of them, ragged and silent, bowing their heads to a thin man in a gray cloak who is not yet certain that he wants to be anyone's lord.

Lin Jian watches from the doorway, with the lamp in his hand.

Above them, in the pine on the east ridge, a cicada starts up.

When the bell begins to ring, he lets go of the lamp.

* * *

Feng finds him sitting on the step of the hut.

He doesn't know how long he's been there. The bell has stopped. The light is going. Lin Feng comes across the yard on a crutch, with his left arm bound to his chest and a purple bruise the size of a dinner plate showing at his collar, and lowers himself with a grunt onto the stone beside him.

For a time they just sit.

"I didn't ask," says Feng.

"What?"

"What you did. With the ring. I saw the pit. I saw the woman go down. Somebody put a pin through that gray bastard's skull from eighty paces, and it wasn't my father." He is looking at his boots. "I didn't ask Aunt Su about that, either. I'm not going to ask. I thought you should know."

"Thank you."

"He called you something. At the end. Grandfather. I heard it from the gate." He hesitates. "Little builder."

"Yes."

Lin Feng nods slowly. He does not say anything else. He sits with his bad arm held against his ribs and his sword across his knees, looking out at the yard where thirty-one people are quietly picking up the pieces of a battle. Then he reaches out, awkwardly, with his good hand, and cuffs Lin Jian on the back of the head, much too gently.

"Go and lie down, radish," he says. "You look like a ghost."

"You look worse."

"I'm not the one who's going to fall off a step." But he is almost smiling.

He goes, in the end, because Feng will not leave until he does. Halfway across the yard he passes the well, and Old Hu is sitting on its stone rim with the bent rod across his knees and a pair of tongs in his hand, as if he cannot decide whether to mend the thing or bury it. His eyes are red. His apron hangs in strips.

"It didn't break," says Hu, without looking up. "Iron that thick. Folded a hundred times. I made it to take a blow from a man like that." He turns it over. "It took it. That is all it was for."

"Hu..."

"I will carve him a stone," says Hu. "With the spirit-iron knife. It's the only thing I own that's fit." He wipes his nose on his wrist. "Go to bed, boy. You and I have work, later. A great deal of work."

* * *

It is close to midnight when Mother comes.

Lin Jian is lying in his own bed, in his own small room, with his arm propped on a cushion and the Light Orb turned down to a coal. He is not asleep. She knows that. She sits down on the edge of the mattress, in her working short robe, with her hair loose, and for a while she doesn't say anything, only looks at him in the dark.

"The woman talked," she says at last.

Lin Jian turns his head.

"Mostly about herself. Where she came from, who hired her, how much. Two hundred stones apiece, and the chain man's second payment on arrival." She is speaking low and even, in the careful voice she uses for reports. "She had no notion of the larger plan. A mercenary. But she was at Red Ridge for three days before the attack, in the east wing, because Qian put the hired men there. And she saw something."

"Wenhai."

"He was in a locked room. At the end of the east corridor, with a Zhao guard at the door. They questioned him every night. About the ring, about the pins, about the hill. She heard some of it through the wall." Mother's hand lies very still on the coverlet. "Then four nights before the attack, he wasn't there."

"Four nights."

"The door was open. The room was empty. No one would say where he'd gone." A breath. "The guard that night was Qian's own man. And the next morning, she says, Zhao Qian came down to breakfast with mud on his boots to the knee, and blisters on both palms, the kind you get from a shovel."

The room is very quiet.

Four days. He thinks of Zhao Heng standing in the sun, with his hands behind his back. My steward is in your custody. And Heng, smiling: Your uncle is a lonely man with a gift for arithmetic. He is my guest.

"He was already dead," says Lin Jian.

"I think so."

"When Heng stood at our gate and said he had a petition in Wenhai's own hand..." He stops. "He knew."

"He knew." Mother's voice has no inflection at all. "Somewhere between here and Red Ridge, your uncle is in the ground, Jian. Under a bush, or in a ditch, in a place where he can be found when someone wants him to be found. And I want to know who Zhao Heng means them to blame."
